planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown crowns in moist, alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in part to full shade in spring; avoid acidic soils.

directions: This heirloom English selection of hart's tongue fern bears much narrower, seaweed-like strap fronds than the typical species, each edged with a gently crenate, stitched-looking margin. Clumps stay compact and slow-spreading, making it a good choice for small shaded rock gardens or trough plantings where the standard broad-leaved form would be too large. Like all hart's tongue ferns it demands calcium-rich, alkaline to neutral soil and declines quickly if grown acidic. Divide established crowns in spring to increase stock.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all frost danger in humid, filtered-light sites; grow in containers or under glass where winters drop below the mid-20s F.

directions: Native to the wet eastern forests of Australia, jungle brake fern forms an upright clump of long, slender, deeply divided deep-green fronds that give it a more delicate, tropical texture than the related Pteris cretica. It wants constant soil moisture, high humidity, and filtered or dappled light, scorching if exposed to direct midday sun and collapsing if the root zone dries out. In frost-free subtropical gardens it makes an excellent shaded understory accent; elsewhere it performs well as a container or conservatory specimen that can summer outdoors in shade. Remove spent fronds at the base to keep the clump tidy.

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded, humid spot only after nights stay reliably above 55F; otherwise grow as a year-round container or conservatory fern.

directions: Unlike most maidenhairs, this tropical American species is a true giant of the genus, producing stout, glossy black-stalked fronds that can reach two to three feet on mature plants, each stalk branching repeatedly into lacy, pale-green pinnae. It is a classic deep-shade understory fern of humid forests and needs consistently moist, humus-rich soil along with high ambient humidity; dry air causes rapid leaf scorch. Grow outdoors only in frost-free, humid climates, or keep as a striking large-scale terrarium, greenhouse, or shaded patio container fern in cooler regions. Divide clumps carefully in spring, since the brittle black stipes snap easily.

planting.note: Plant in consistently moist, shaded ground only in frost-free zones; elsewhere grow in containers and protect from frost.

directions: Also sold as silver lace fern (and formerly classified as Pteris straminea), this fast-growing clumping brake fern has finely cut, slightly cupped, lacy fronds that give it an airy texture well suited to groundcover plantings under shaded eaves or along damp garden paths. It spreads readily by rhizome in warm, humid gardens but is killed by any real frost, so northern growers treat it as a container or houseplant that summers outdoors in shade. Keep the soil evenly moist; fronds brown quickly at the tips if allowed to dry out, and once crisped they will not recover.

planting.note: Set out in dappled shade and humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil once frost danger has passed; in cold climates keep as a greenhouse or terrarium fern.

directions: This small East Asian and Australasian maidenhair earns its 'walking' nickname from the way new plantlets root readily from offsets at the frond bases, letting an established patch creep outward across moist, shaded ground. The dark-green, bristly-textured fronds are finer and more delicate than those of the common Adiantum species, and the plant is correspondingly fussier about humidity, scorching if the air or soil dries out. Best grown in dappled light in a frost-free shade garden, terrarium, or hanging basket of free-draining, humus-rich mix. Tidy the clump each year by removing old fronds just before new spring growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant in deep, moist shade with reliable shelter from drying wind; grows well in cool, damp microclimates near buildings but resents hard freezes.

directions: This New Zealand forest-floor maidenhair produces erect fronds whose new growth emerges a soft orange-gold before maturing to a deep, soft mid-green, giving the plant seasonal color interest unusual among maidenhairs. It is an understory species of cool, constantly damp native bush and performs best in deep shade with humus-rich, evenly moist, free-draining soil, tolerating cooler conditions than many tropical Adiantum species but still intolerant of hard frost or dry air. Good for shaded courtyards, fern gardens, or large terrariums. Propagation is slow from freshly sown spores, so most gardeners start from nursery-grown divisions.

planting.note: Tuck small plants into rock crevices, walls, or gritty troughs with sharp drainage in part sun to light shade.

directions: This miniature fern — found naturally in rocky ravines from the Himalayas to the mountains of southern Arizona and northern Mexico — forms tiny tufted rosettes of leathery, scaly-backed fronds only a few inches tall. Unlike most shade ferns on this list, it is adapted to intermittent dryness between rains and wants sharp drainage in a lean, gritty mix, rotting if kept constantly wet. Best suited to crevice gardens, dry-stacked stone walls, troughs, or rock garden pockets in part sun to light shade, where its diminutive scale makes it a conversation piece rather than a mass planting fern. Protect from prolonged hard freezes in colder parts of its hardiness range.
